value.overview: The Buffy-crowned Wood-Partridge (Dendrortyx leucophrys) is a secretive New World quail of humid mountain forests in Middle America. It spends most of its time on or near the forest floor, where it moves through dense vegetation in pairs or small family groups. Its loud, far-carrying calls often reveal its presence before the bird is seen. Costa Rica supports a resident population, especially in the country's cool, wet central highlands and adjacent mountain ranges.
value.classification: The species belongs to the family Odontophoridae, the New World quails, within the order Galliformes. The Costa Rican population is generally treated as the subspecies Dendrortyx leucophrys hypospodius.
value.identification: This plump, long-tailed partridge is about 28–30 cm long. It has a buffy to chestnut crown and short crest, a pale face and throat, reddish-brown upperparts, and a blue-gray to dark gray underbody marked with chestnut or darker streaking. A conspicuous bare red area surrounds the eye. It is usually detected by its loud, rapid, hoarse whistles rather than by direct observation, because it remains concealed in thick ground vegetation.
value.rangeHabitat: The Buffy-crowned Wood-Partridge occurs from southern Mexico through Central America to Costa Rica and western Panama. In Costa Rica it is a resident of the higher, wetter parts of the Central Valley and nearby slopes of the Central Volcanic and Talamanca ranges, including the Dota region and Cerro de la Muerte massif. It inhabits humid montane evergreen, cloud, and oak forests, as well as dense second growth, forest edges, bamboo or brushy thickets, ravines, and some partly disturbed highland habitats, generally at middle to high elevations.
value.migrationStatus: It is a year-round resident in Costa Rica and is not considered a long-distance migrant. Local movements between elevations may occur, but regular seasonal migration is not known.
value.breeding: Breeding records indicate nesting during the wetter-season months, broadly from February through June in parts of the range, although timing can vary with elevation and local conditions. The nest is placed on or near the ground in dense vegetation and may be a domed structure or a concealed depression lined with plant material. Clutches commonly contain about six or seven eggs. Chicks are precocial and remain with the adults after hatching, usually as part of a small family group.
value.dietFeeding: The species forages mainly on the ground, scratching through leaf litter and soil beneath forest cover. Its diet includes seeds, buds, berries and other small fruits, and a variety of invertebrates. Feeding is generally carried out in dense understory, where the birds can quickly retreat from danger. Seasonal changes in fruit, seeds, and invertebrate abundance probably influence local movements and the size of groups.
value.behavior: Buffy-crowned Wood-Partridges are secretive, terrestrial birds that commonly travel in pairs or family groups of roughly four to six individuals; larger coveys may form outside the breeding period. They often stay hidden while walking through leaf litter and thick understory. Their distinctive calls are most frequent around dawn and again near dusk, and neighboring birds may answer one another from within the forest. They can run rapidly through cover and usually flush only at close range.
